speaker_role: independent counselor (Kevin, self-described Yale grad and college counselor, ElevatEd School)
commercial_incentive: explicitly promotes his own paid essay-editing service (elevated.school/editmyessay) with a discount code at the end
key_insights: At a major college admissions conference, most AI use by colleges was on the business/enrollment-marketing side (chatbots, funnel automation) rather than in evaluating applicants.

Virginia Tech reportedly uses AI to cut essay readers from two per file to one, with AI helping 'triage' the load while humans still review every file - presenter flags this as a concerning trend toward less human review over time.
UNC Charlotte reportedly piloted AI specifically to flag grammar/writing-style issues in essays; presenter raises concern this could unfairly penalize ESL students for minor errors.
Representatives from top/elite schools (Yale, Columbia, UCLA, Carnegie Mellon) stated they do not use AI to evaluate applications and that a human always makes the final admissions decision.
Most colleges reportedly do not rely on AI-detection tools to screen essays because of high false-positive/hallucination rates, per a GW admissions officer cited by the presenter.

Admissions officers at the conference said using AI to brainstorm or polish an essay is acceptable (comparable to getting help from a family member or teacher), but writing the essay outright with AI is easily detected, and an inconsistent 'voice' across parts of an application (e.g., a required writing sample) can raise red flags.
Flags overuse of certain 'AI-coded' words (e.g., 'tapestry') and heavy em-dash use as patterns that may read as AI-generated to reviewers and should be minimized.

Notes admissions officers reportedly encourage high school counselors to use AI to help draft recommendation letters (e.g., feeding it past letters and student brag sheets), since counselors often write 200-300 letters in a short winter-break window.
specific_numbers_or_facts: The word 'tapestry' appeared in fewer than 50 essays five years ago versus more than 500 times last year, per a GW admissions officer cited by the presenter
Counselors reportedly writing 200-300 recommendation letters within a 2-3 week span over winter break, per admissions officers cited by the presenter
Virginia Tech reportedly reduced its essay readers from two per file to one, per the presenter's conference notes
notable_or_distinctive: The specific, named 'tapestry' word-frequency anecdote and the Virginia Tech two-readers-to-one detail are unusually concrete, source-attributed claims rather than generic AI-ethics advice.
reliability_notes: All claims are the presenter's secondhand summary of conference panel statements without direct quotes or citations to verify; individual schools' internal AI practices cannot be independently confirmed from the transcript, and the video closes with a paid essay-editing service promotion.
